title: Athletes Keep Disappearing at the Commonwealth Games — Glasgow 2026 Is No Exception
excerpt: Four Ugandan boxers vanished from their team hotel after the Games ended, continuing a decades-long pattern that has seen more than 400 athletes abscond from Commonwealth events since 2002.
body:
• Four Ugandan boxers — Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis, and Emily Nakalema — vanished after the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, reportedly intending to seek asylum in the UK.
  • Reports also indicate a Pakistani boxer went missing from the team hotel during the Games, according to NDTV Sports and India Today.
  • More than 400 athletes, coaches, and officials have absconded from Commonwealth Games events since 2002, including 230 from the 2018 Gold Coast Games alone.
  • Glasgow 2026 had no athletes' village, with teams housed in hotels, raising pre-Games concerns about security and tracking.

The 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow ended on August 2 with closing ceremonies and medal tallies. Within 48 hours, a different kind of story emerged: athletes had gone missing.

Four members of Uganda's boxing team — Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis, and Emily Nakalema — failed to meet their teammates for the scheduled return flight home, according to Ugandan publication NBS Sports. Speaking anonymously, one of the missing boxers told NBS that all four intend to seek asylum in the United Kingdom, citing a desire for better training facilities and career opportunities.

Separately, NDTV Sports and India Today reported that a Pakistani boxer also went missing after leaving the team hotel during the Games, though details about the individual's identity and circumstances remain limited.

A Pattern Spanning Two Decades

The disappearances are far from unusual. At least 400 athletes, coaches, officials, and accompanying family members have absconded from Commonwealth Games events since 2002, according to a count compiled by British media.

The numbers are striking in their consistency. At the 2002 Manchester Games, 27 people failed to return, including 21 members of the Sierra Leone delegation. Melbourne 2006 saw 40 disappearances. Glasgow, when it last hosted in 2014, recorded 66 absconders, including two Ugandan rugby players, two Cameroonian wrestlers, and a Sierra Leonean sprinter.

The problem escalated dramatically at the 2018 Gold Coast Games in Australia, where 230 individuals from multiple African nations vanished. Birmingham 2022 saw 17 go missing, including two Pakistani boxers — one of whom, Nazeer Khan, was later found working in a kebab shop in Scotland and was convicted of stalking a local woman.

"These staggering figures will alarm Glaswegians about a similar situation occurring."

— Annie Wells, Scottish Conservative MSP, before the Games

No Athletes' Village, No Easy Oversight

Glasgow's 2026 edition was a slimmed-down affair from the start. After the Australian state of Victoria withdrew as original host in 2023, citing projected costs exceeding A$6 billion, Glasgow stepped in with a reduced program of 10 sports — down from 19 at Birmingham 2022. Around 3,000 athletes competed from 74 Commonwealth nations and territories between July 23 and August 2.

Crucially, no athletes' village was constructed. Teams were housed in hotels across the city, a decision that had sparked pre-Games warnings from Scottish politicians about the difficulty of monitoring athlete movements. "Organisers must ensure everyone who comes here to compete is accounted for," Conservative MSP Annie Wells said before the Games began.

Asylum, Opportunity, and the Limits of Sport

The Ugandan boxers who spoke to NBS Sports framed their decision in terms that reflect a recurring tension at Commonwealth events: athletes from developing nations using the Games as a route to countries with more resources and opportunities. The four boxers appealed to Ugandans "for understanding" and asked "not to be judged."

For South Asian delegations, the pattern has its own history. Pakistan has seen athletes disappear at multiple Games, and the broader phenomenon touches on questions about visa access, economic opportunity, and the gap between what international sport promises and what it delivers for athletes from less wealthy nations.

Officials in Glasgow are currently working with Ugandan and other national delegations to locate the missing athletes. The UK's Ministry of Education and Sports is expected to release a statement, though previous cases suggest formal searches rarely result in returns — most absconders either claim asylum or remain undetected.
nri_angle: The pattern of South Asian athletes absconding from Commonwealth events raises questions about immigration, opportunity, and the desperation that drives people to seek asylum through sporting events.
